name: Battle of the Nile
info: A British fleet under Rear-Admiral Sir Horatio Nelson attacked the French fleet of Vice-admiral Brueys anchored in Aboukir Bay, Egypt, in August 1798, and destroyed or captured all but four of its ships, leaving Napoleon's army in Egypt cut off.

facts.date: 1 to 3 August 1798; the main fighting began at about 18:20 on 1 August
facts.place: Aboukir Bay, on the Mediterranean coast of Egypt, about 20 miles (32 km) north-east of Alexandria
facts.sides: The Royal Navy under Rear-Admiral Sir Horatio Nelson, with 13 ships of the line, and the French Navy under Vice-admiral François-Paul Brueys d'Aigalliers, with 13 ships of the line and four frigates; 17 French ships were engaged
facts.outcome: Brueys was killed and his flagship Orient blew up; only two French ships of the line and two frigates escaped, and Napoleon's army was left in Egypt without a fleet.

t: Brueys anchored his 13 ships of the line in a line inside the bay, but left room between the leading ship and the shoal, and Nelson's ships passed through it and caught the French vanguard in a crossfire.
Of 17 French ships engaged, two ships of the line and two frigates escaped; the French flagship Orient blew up at about 22:00 with more than 1,000 men killed.
The defeat left Napoleon's army trapped in Egypt and gave the Royal Navy the dominant position in the Mediterranean that it kept for the rest of the Napoleonic Wars.
dyk: Nelson pursued the French for more than two months and passed their invasion convoy in the dark on 22 June, missing it by less than a day when he reached Alexandria on 28 June.
ev: Bonaparte's armada sails from Toulon for Egypt
Nelson's fleet passes the French convoy in the darkness without knowing it
Bonaparte lands in Egypt and takes Alexandria, and Brueys anchors in Aboukir Bay
The British fleet attacks the French at about 18:20 on the 1st and the French flagship Orient explodes at 22:00
Fighting resumes on the 2nd and the last French ship of the line destroyed or captured, Timoléon, blows up on the 3rd
News of the victory reaches Britain and Nelson is made Baron Nelson of the Nile

sections.background:
Napoleon Bonaparte's victories in northern Italy helped secure French victory in the War of the First Coalition in 1797, and Great Britain remained the only major European power still at war with the French Republic. The French navy was dominant in the Mediterranean after the British fleet withdrew following the outbreak of war between Britain and Spain in 1796. Bonaparte proposed invading Egypt, nominally part of the neutral Ottoman Empire, as a staging point for operations against British India. The Directory agreed.

In spring 1798 Bonaparte assembled more than 35,000 soldiers and a fleet at Toulon, and kept the destination secret. The armada sailed on 19 May, took Malta between 9 and 12 June, and left for Alexandria on 19 June. Nelson, a rear-admiral, was sent from the Tagus by Earl St. Vincent to investigate. He had ten ships of the line and a fourth-rate under Captain Thomas Troubridge by 7 June, but no intelligence of the French destination and no frigates. Having decided that Egypt was the target, he passed the slow French convoy in darkness on 22 June, reached Alexandria on 28 June, found nothing and turned back. French scouts arrived there on the evening of 29 June.

Bonaparte landed and took Alexandria. His naval commander, Vice-admiral Brueys, found the harbour channel too shallow and narrow for the larger ships and chose Aboukir Bay. Nelson learned of the landing at Coron on 28 July and turned south, and on the afternoon of 1 August his scouts sighted the French transports at Alexandria.
sections.forces:
Each fleet had 13 ships of the line, but most historians conclude that the French were marginally more powerful. Culloden ran aground, Orient was much larger than Leander, the 50-gun ship of the British force, and the French had two frigates and several smaller vessels in the action. Spartiate, Franklin, Orient, Tonnant and Guillaume Tell were each significantly larger than any single British ship. Brueys flew his flag in the 120-gun Orient at the centre of the line, Counter-admiral Armand Blanquet was in Franklin, and Counter-admiral Pierre-Charles Villeneuve commanded the rear division in Guillaume Tell.

Brueys anchored his 13 ships of the line along the north-eastern edge of the shoals, 160 yards (150 m) apart, the line 2,850 yards (2,610 m) long, with four frigates in an inner line. He hoped the shoals would force the British to attack his strong centre and rear while his vanguard used the north-easterly wind to counterattack. He left room between the leading ship, Guerrier, and the shoal for an enemy ship to cross the head of the line, and the French prepared only their seaward guns: on the port side the gun ports were closed and the decks uncleared.

The fleet was short of food and water, and up to a third of the sailors were ashore foraging at any time. Nelson's plan was to pass down the seaward side of the French van and centre so that each French ship would face two British ships and Orient three. Each British ship was to show four horizontal lights and a White Ensign, so that ships would not fire on one another in the dark.
sections.course:
At 14:00 on 1 August, lookouts on Zealous reported the French in Aboukir Bay. Brueys had no scouts out and recalled his shore parties, though most had not returned when the battle began. He ordered the line to set sail, then cancelled the order when Nelson slowed his leading ships at 16:00 to rig springs on their anchor cables. The British had no charts of the bay beyond a rough sketch and two inaccurate maps. At 18:20 the leading French ships Guerrier and Conquérant opened fire on Goliath and Zealous.

Captain Thomas Foley in Goliath noticed the gap between Guerrier and the shoal and, on his own initiative, crossed the head of the line, raking Guerrier down its unprepared port side. Hood in Zealous anchored beside Guerrier, whose foremast fell within five minutes. Orion, Theseus and Audacious also crossed or passed inside the line, and Vanguard, Minotaur and Defence anchored on the seaward side at 18:40. Culloden ran onto the shoal in the growing darkness. Guerrier and Spartiate surrendered at 21:00. At about 20:30 Nelson was struck over his blinded right eye by a splinter and carried below, but the surgeon found a flesh wound.

Bellerophon, under the main battery of Orient, lost her masts and cut her cables at 20:20. Brueys was struck by a cannonball and died fifteen minutes later. At 21:00 a fire was seen on Orient's lower decks, and at 22:00 it reached the magazines and the ship was destroyed by an explosion. Franklin resumed firing after a ten-minute lull and was forced to surrender. By midnight only Tonnant remained engaged.
sections.aftermath:
Firing broke out again at 04:00 on 2 August between the French southern division and the British ships Alexander and Majestic, soon joined by Goliath and Theseus. Heureux and Mercure, which had cut their cables to escape the explosion of Orient, drifted onto the shoal and surrendered within minutes. Guillaume Tell, Généreux, Justice and Diane stood out to sea, pursued by Zealous. On 3 August Tonnant surrendered, with 1,600 survivors from other French vessels on board, and Timoléon was set on fire by its crew and exploded shortly after midday, the eleventh and final French ship of the line destroyed or captured.

British casualties were recorded as 218 killed and approximately 677 wounded, though the number of wounded who later died is not known. French casualties are harder to calculate; estimates range from 2,000 to 5,000, with a suggested median of 3,500, including more than 1,000 captured and wounded and nearly 2,000 killed, half of them on Orient. Brueys was killed, Blanquet wounded, and four captains died. Two ships of the line and two frigates were destroyed, and three captured ships were too battered ever to sail again.

Nelson stayed at anchor for two weeks, recovering from his head wound. The first message reached Bonaparte on 14 August, and he later blamed the wounded Blanquet, falsely accusing him of surrendering Franklin while his ship was undamaged. Nelson's first dispatches were lost when Leander was defeated by Généreux off Crete on 18 August, so news reached Britain only on 2 October.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from the despatches, letters and memoirs of its participants and from later histories. Nelson's letters record his search for the French. Brueys wrote to the Minister of Marine about the weakness of his crews and rigging, and Seaman John Nicol of Goliath described the bay the morning after, covered with dead bodies. King George III's speech to Parliament is recorded in William James's naval history of 1827, and Napoleon's later comment on Villeneuve from his Mémoires. Two accounts of how Bonaparte took the news differ: one has him read the report without emotion, and Bourienne, his secretary, has him almost overcome.

Archaeology adds to the written record. In 1983 a French survey team under Jacques Dumas found the wreck of Orient, and in 1998 Franck Goddio led a major project in the bay, finding material scattered over 500 metres and evidence of two explosions. He recovered coins from across the Mediterranean, probably part of the treasure taken from Malta. In 2000 Paolo Gallo's excavation on Nelson's Island found graves dating from the battle.

How the fire on Orient began has never been firmly established. One common account is that jars of oil and paint left on the poop deck were ignited by burning wadding from a British ship; Fleet Captain Honoré Ganteaume reported instead an explosion on the quarterdeck, preceded by minor fires among the boats. French losses survive only as a range, and historians debate the comparative strength of the fleets.
sections.legacy:
The battle reversed the strategic situation in the Mediterranean. The Royal Navy returned in force and blockaded French and allied ports, and the siege of Malta lasted two years before the French defenders were starved into surrender. British ships played a crucial part in Bonaparte's defeat at the siege of Acre in 1799, after which he returned to France without his army, leaving Kléber in command of Egypt. The Ottoman Empire was encouraged to go to war with France, and the Austrian and Russian empires declared war in 1799 as part of a Second Coalition. A British expeditionary force defeated the remains of the French army in Egypt in 1801.

Nelson was made Baron Nelson of the Nile and Burnham Thorpe, a title with which he was privately dissatisfied. Each captain received a gold medal, and the Ottoman Emperor Selim III made him a Knight Commander of the new Order of the Crescent. On 29 September 1798 he described his officers as "We few, we happy few, we band of brothers", from which grew the idea of the Nelsonic Band of Brothers. Some have called the battle "arguably, the most decisive naval engagement of the great age of sail". Edward Ingram noted that the campaign has sometimes been considered a strategic success for France, since Bonaparte was free to continue the war in the Middle East.

The battle is remembered in cartoons, paintings, poems and plays, among them Felicia Hemans's poem Casabianca of 1826, about the death of the captain's son on Orient. Cleopatra's Needle in London, given by Muhammad Ali of Egypt in 1819, was raised on the Victoria Embankment in 1878.

summary: Between 1 and 3 August 1798 a British fleet under Nelson attacked the French fleet anchored in Aboukir Bay, killed its commander Brueys, and destroyed or captured 11 of its 13 ships of the line. The defeat left Napoleon's army in Egypt cut off and gave Britain control of the Mediterranean.
notes: The lead and Aftermath say Brueys' ships numbered 13 ships of the line plus frigates; the lead says 17 ships were engaged in total and only two ships of the line and two frigates escaped.
Ship counts: 'eleventh and final French ship of the line destroyed or captured' (Timoléon) and 13 in total, consistent with two escaping.
Spartiate's surrender is given at 21:00; Conquérant's time is only 'before 19:00' for the masts, so I wrote 'earlier'.
Order of the Crescent is given as 'newly created'; the Needle's date of gift 1819 is as the article states.
The article says the battle's date fully as 1 to 3 August; the ev entry for 'Early July' is my wording for the landing after 29 June; the article gives no exact date for the landing.

Left out: the Casabianca boy's death in detail, the anecdote of toothpicks and snuffbox, Lady Hamilton's fainting, the Nile Clumps and other tree memorials, Smiley's People, prize values and renamings, Nelson's quoted remarks, the French press reaction and Villeneuve's defence.

The article says 'decisively defeated' in its lead; I quote 'arguably, the most decisive naval engagement of the great age of sail' attributed in the text only as 'some historians' (the article does not name who).
Sentence about Orient and Leander: article says 'the relative sizes of Orient and Leander'; I wrote Leander was the 50-gun ship, which the article gives in the Culloden passage.
